metadata.title: Enhancing middle school science education: Evaluating a competency-based STEM training program for teachers

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design with 48 science teachers from middle schools in the capital of Oman (grades 5–7). The analysis was conducted with IBM SPSS using Two-Way MANOVA and follow-up univariate ANOVAs; the manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or any ILSA-style replicate weights. Because the data are a small, recruited teacher sample rather than an international large-scale assessment microdata file, standard student sampling weights are not described, and the results should be interpreted as program-evaluation effects within the study sample. No PV scaling or IRT/WLE procedures are involved; the primary measurement is a scenario-based teacher PCK test (TPCKST) scored on a 1–3 scale.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variables are teachers’ scores on a scenario-based Pedagogical Content Knowledge of STEM test (TPCKST), not cognitive achievement scales from an ILSA that generate PVs. Missing-data handling is not reported because the manuscript does not describe any missingness protocol (e.g., exclusion rules, imputation, or complete-case criteria) for TPCKST items or pre/post scores. Given the small sample size (48 teachers), the absence of a documented missing-data strategy is a transparency gap for interpreting robustness of the reported pretest equivalence and posttest effects.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were recruited from middle schools in the capital of Oman (junior high schools) between November and December 2023. Inclusion criteria required teachers to have at least five years of teaching experience, to teach science students in grades 5–7, and to work in the capital; teachers were then randomly assigned to experimental (n=24) and control (n=24) groups. The experimental group received a three-week competency-based STEM training program; the control group continued regular professional development without STEM integration/engineering design emphasis. The manuscript does not report any additional item-level exclusions, missing-score rules, or complete-case criteria for TPCKST scoring.

main_findings.dataset_used: Oman teacher PCK (TPCKST) pretest–posttest; grades 5–7 science; scenario-based STEM PCK test
main_findings.performance_metrics: Post-hoc univariate ANOVA: EXP M=6.00 (SD=1.62) vs CON M=4.79 (SD=1.56), F(1, 44)=6.81, p<0.05, partial η2=0.13; baseline equivalence: t(46)=0.82, p=0.430
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Oman teacher PCK (TPCKST) pretest–posttest data for grades 5–7 science, the study leveraged training group and teacher gender to predict teaching procedures (Q1) scores, finding that the experimental group scored significantly higher than the control group after training (F(1, 44)=6.81, p<0.05, partial η2=0.13). This indicates that competency-based STEM professional development can improve teachers’ planning and execution of STEM-aligned teaching procedures, though causality is limited by the small quasi-experimental sample and the lack of reported missing-data handling.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Oman teacher PCK (TPCKST) pretest–posttest data for grades 5–7 science, the study leveraged training group and teacher gender to predict teaching planning (Q2) scores, finding that the experimental group scored significantly higher than the control group after training (F(1, 44)=6.77, p<0.05, partial η2=0.13). This indicates that STEM-focused teacher training supports stronger lesson planning aligned with engineering design and interdisciplinary approaches, though the findings should be generalized cautiously beyond the capital-city teacher sample.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Oman teacher PCK (TPCKST) pretest–posttest data for grades 5–7 science, the study leveraged training group and teacher gender to predict content knowledge (Q3) scores, finding that the experimental group scored significantly higher than the control group after training (F(1, 44)=8.63, p<0.01, partial η2=0.16). This indicates that competency-based STEM training can deepen teachers’ STEM content understanding in ways that support classroom instruction, though the study’s small sample and unreported missing-data strategy limit certainty about effect stability.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Post-hoc univariate ANOVA: EXP M=7.83 (SD=0.38) vs CON M=6.87 (SD=1.08), F(1, 44)=17.37, p<0.001, partial η2=0.28; baseline equivalence: t(46)=1.40, p=0.168
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Oman teacher PCK (TPCKST) pretest–posttest data for grades 5–7 science, the study leveraged training group and teacher gender to predict methods of correcting misconceptions (Q4) scores, finding that the experimental group scored significantly higher than the control group after training (F(1, 44)=17.37, p<0.001, partial η2=0.28). This indicates that misconception-focused components of STEM professional development may be especially effective for improving teachers’ diagnostic and remediation practices, which is likely to strengthen students’ conceptual learning, while causality remains constrained by the quasi-experimental design and missing-data transparency.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Post-hoc univariate ANOVA: EXP M=4.75 (SD=1.42) vs CON M=5.08 (SD=0.79), F(1, 44)=5.07, p=0.029, partial η2=0.103; baseline equivalence: t(46)=-1.81, p=0.078
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Oman teacher PCK (TPCKST) pretest–posttest data for grades 5–7 science, the study leveraged training group and teacher gender to predict methods of teaching (Q5) scores, finding a statistically significant group effect in the posttest (F(1, 44)=5.07, p=0.029, partial η2=0.103). This indicates that the training may influence teachers’ instructional methods, but the direction and practical magnitude should be interpreted carefully given the reported means and the modest effect size.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Post-hoc univariate ANOVA: EXP M=7.50 (SD=0.78) vs CON M=6.25 (SD=1.82), F(1, 44)=9.13, p<0.01, partial η2=0.17; baseline equivalence: t(46)=-1.06, p=0.297
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Oman teacher PCK (TPCKST) pretest–posttest data for grades 5–7 science, the study leveraged training group and teacher gender to predict assessment (Q6) scores, finding that the experimental group scored significantly higher than the control group after training (F(1, 44)=9.13, p<0.01, partial η2=0.17). This indicates that STEM professional development can improve teachers’ assessment practices aligned with STEM learning goals, supporting more formative and misconception-aware instruction, though generalization is limited by the small capital-city sample and unreported missing-data handling.

data.outcome_summary: This quasi-experimental teacher program evaluation used a scenario-based STEM Pedagogical Content Knowledge test (TPCKST) administered to 48 science teachers in Oman’s capital (grades 5–7 focus). Teachers were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n=24) receiving a three-week competency-based STEM training program (engineering design, inquiry-based learning, collaborative workshops, and reflection) or a control group (n=24) continuing regular professional development without STEM integration emphasis. Baseline equivalence was supported by non-significant pretest differences across six TPCKST domains. Post-intervention, a two-way MANOVA showed a significant overall group effect (Wilks’ Lambda=0.52, F(6,39)=5.99, p<0.001, partial η2=0.48), with univariate ANOVAs indicating significant improvements for Q1–Q4 and Q6 (largest effect for correcting misconceptions, Q4: partial η2=0.28). The study reports no survey weights and does not document missing-data handling, so robustness and external validity beyond the capital-city sample should be interpreted cautiously.
